preamble.text: Historical snapshot: later evidence may be reflected in current research pages and corrections.
Deterministically compiled from canonical evidence. Importance measures impact, not truth; evidence/confidence remain separate.

blocks.text: 1. EgoWild2Dex reports transferring in-the-wild human video to bimanual robot manipulation with limited robot data

Desk: multimodality_world_models Evidence: A · credible_unconfirmed · developing · importance 6/10 (Major) Importance rationale: If the reported transfer and data-efficiency results generalize, natural human demonstrations could reduce robot-specific data collection for dexterous manipulation. Score 6 reflects potential importance to embodied-model training; the current evidence is one paper on three tasks and does not establish broad transfer or remove robot fine-tuning.

What changed: The authors present EgoWild2Dex, which aligns egocentric human observations with robot views and trains a dexterous manipulation policy through broad human-data pretraining, task-specific human–robot co-training and robot-domain refinement. Their EgoWild corpus contains 538.9 hours, 179,049 episodes and 125,961 task descriptions. On three long-horizon bimanual tasks, the authors report 90%–100% success using less than one hour of robot demonstrations per task; object-level success on three unseen package contents is 30%–40%. GeoFormer image alignment is reported at 7.43 ms mean latency versus 162.58 ms for a projection-and-inpainting baseline, excluding image decoding and model loading. These are author-reported results from a limited task and robot setting; the paper says the data, models and code will be released and still requires robot fine-tuning. Why it matters: The work tests a path from large, naturally collected human manipulation data to dexterous robot behavior with limited task-specific robot demonstrations. If the transfer holds beyond three tasks and the reported dataset becomes accessible, it could change the data and collection-cost requirements for bimanual manipulation. Current results still depend on robot fine-tuning, specific hands and a staged training pipeline, and do not establish broad zero-shot robot transfer.

Demonstrated: The paper specifies an in-the-wild corpus, staged training method and author-run real-robot and alignment evaluations. Measurements and success rates remain paper-reported and were not independently reproduced.

Claimed: Authors report 90%–100% success across three long-horizon bimanual tasks using less than one hour of robot demonstrations per task. Three unseen object categories yield 30%–40% success (33.3% mean). GeoFormer has 7.43 ms mean and 12.97 ms P95 latency versus 162.58 ms and 194.16 ms for projection plus inpainting; estimated processing cost is 2.06 versus 45.16 GPU-hours per million frames.

Mechanism: EgoWild2Dex first trains on unscripted egocentric human manipulation data, then aligns task-specific human views with robot views using GeoFormer, co-trains on aligned human, glove and limited robot demonstrations, and refines on robot execution/recovery data. Human and robot actions are retargeted into a shared robot-native action space.

Strongest baseline: For full-policy task results, direct fine-tuning of π₀, π₀.₅ and GR00T-N1.7 has much lower success under the paper's protocol. For image alignment, GeoFormer is compared with MoGe projection plus LaMa inpainting; task success on Open-Box is 90% versus 80%, with faster reported processing. These are author-run comparisons, not independent matched replications.

Regime: 538.9 hours of egocentric human data (179,049 episodes); three long-horizon bimanual tasks; less than one hour of robot demonstrations per task plus task-specific human/glove demonstrations and robot-domain refinement. Object transfer is tested on three unseen package contents. GeoFormer timings exclude image decode and model loading.

Limitations: All results are author-reported; no independent reproduction or artifact run occurred in this activation.; The full pipeline requires task-specific human–robot co-training and real-robot fine-tuning; human demonstrations alone remain insufficient for the reported long-horizon tasks.; Reported task success covers three tasks and specific dual-arm/hand setups. Zero-shot object success is 33.3% averaged across three unseen package contents, not broad zero-shot task transfer.; GeoFormer timing excludes image decoding and model loading; the dataset and models were not confirmed publicly accessible during this review.; The paper notes GeoFormer cannot recover visual content moved outside the camera field of view and leaves higher-DoF hand validation open.

Open evidence gaps: No independent reproduction was performed and public release of the data, code and model weights was not confirmed in this review.; The end-to-end success results cover three tasks and specific robot embodiments; broader task, hand and site transfer is not established.; The full method uses task-specific human and robot data and robot-domain refinement; the paper does not establish that human demonstrations alone suffice.
Sources: https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.23755
2. WaveletECO reports a specialized local model matching a frontier API on chip-repair scores at lower estimated inference cost

Desk: efficiency Evidence: A · credible_unconfirmed · developing · importance 6/10 (Major) Importance rationale: If the benchmark and inference-cost results generalize, specialized local models could alter the cost and provider-dependence trade-off for physical chip repair workflows. Score 6 reflects potential importance to a high-cost engineering domain, not truth or transfer beyond the tested designs.

What changed: The authors combine a closed-loop engineering-change-order workflow with a Qwen3.5-9B model trained on repair demonstrations and action preferences. Across 22 chip designs and 594 runs, they report a mean repair score of 79.65 for INT8 and 79.63 for BF16, versus 77.44 for GPT-6 Astra under a shared execution protocol. Their cost model estimates INT8 inference at $0.00226 per task versus $0.33188 for GPT-6 Astra, about 1/147 as much, excluding EDA and idle costs. These are author-reported results from one benchmark; nine designs are held out, but the broader generalization and deployment economics remain unverified. Why it matters: If the reported quality and cost estimates transfer to larger design sets and production workflows, a specialized local model could make multi-round physical chip repair cheaper while reducing dependence on paid frontier APIs. The reported cost ratio concerns inference only and uses estimated local GPU rental and throughput; it does not establish end-to-end EDA economics or a general advantage over frontier models.

Demonstrated: The inspected paper documents the workflow, benchmark protocol, score definition, author-reported measurements and cost model. Neither performance nor cost was independently reproduced in this activation.

Claimed: In 594 runs over 22 designs (three repeats for each of nine model variants per design), WaveletECO-Policy INT8 scores 79.65 and BF16 79.63, versus GPT-6 Astra 77.44 under the shared protocol. INT8 estimated inference cost is $0.00226/task versus $0.33188/task for GPT-6 Astra, a modeled 146.8× score-per-dollar comparison.

Mechanism: A shared physical ECO workflow reads timing, electrical and library state, selects a repair action, executes and measures it, then retains accepted changes or rolls back rejected ones. A local Qwen3.5-9B model is trained with supervised fine-tuning and CPO-SimPO preference data from same-state repair actions; quantized variants use INT8 or INT4 weights with BF16 activations.

Strongest baseline: GPT-6 Astra scored 77.44 under the same ECO execution interface across the same design set. The authors also compare local Qwen3.5-9B direct and thinking variants, WaveletECO SFT, GPT-5.6 Sol and DeepSeek V4. The quality score and cost estimate are not a matched deployment comparison because cost-estimation deployments were not re-evaluated for repair quality.

Regime: 22 physical chip designs, 13 used for adaptation/model selection and nine held out; up to five repair rounds; three repeats per model/design; one candidate action per round and 1% area-growth limit. Local inference-cost estimates use single GPUs (BF16 on RTX 6000D, INT8/INT4 on RTX 4090); API reference prices were recorded September 19, 2026.

Open evidence gaps: Repair-quality and cost claims have not been independently reproduced; the cost model is limited to inference and specified September 2026 prices/rental proxies.; Benchmark uses 22 designs from one setting and one EDA backend; transfer across nodes, design types and toolchains is unmeasured.
Sources: https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.23444
3. A mathematical-analysis preprint reports mismatches between OpenAI’s Navier-Stokes proof and cited Lean estimates

Desk: evaluation_science Evidence: A · credible_unconfirmed · active · importance 6/10 (Major) Importance rationale: If the reported mismatches hold, a machine-checked Lean result cannot be treated as verification of the specific natural-language proof without a semantic bridge. This changes how an extraordinary mathematical claim should be evaluated, although the audit does not refute the underlying theorem.

What changed: Bastounis, Circelli and Hansen compare OpenAI’s natural-language Navier–Stokes proof with cited Lean declarations. For Lemma 8.6, equation (8.19), they report that the manuscript states an m+4 derivative estimate while the cited Lean estimate requires m+5. For pressure-flux equation (10.19), they report a different Lean bound and proof route, including an additional localized gradient norm. They note one similar auxiliary bound in the repository does not appear to be directly used in the proposed theorem, leaving the effect on the actual proof dependency chain unresolved. The authors explicitly do not claim the natural-language blow-up proof is incorrect. This remains a source-reported critique in an arXiv preprint, without independent reproduction or established specialist consensus. Why it matters: A formal proof establishes its encoded theorem, but it does not by itself establish that the theorem matches the natural-language argument it is meant to check. The reported estimate differences give concrete targets for independent Lean and PDE review of an extraordinary mathematical claim, while leaving the truth of the underlying blow-up result unresolved.

Claimed: The authors report an m+4 versus m+5 derivative requirement in Lemma 8.6 and a distinct pressure-flux estimate/proof route for equation (10.19), challenging correspondence between selected manuscript arguments and cited Lean declarations.

Mechanism: Compares selected estimates and proof steps in OpenAI’s natural-language Navier–Stokes paper against cited Lean declarations and pinned source revisions. The critique separates encoded theorem validity from semantic fidelity to the written argument.

Strongest baseline: OpenAI’s natural-language paper and its cited Lean declarations are compared directly. The authors report explicit estimate differences but do not claim the natural-language theorem is false; neither the critique nor theorem has independent peer-reviewed resolution in this review.
Regime: Selected analytic estimates in one natural-language Navier-Stokes proof and corresponding Lean declarations; the paper does not audit every proof dependency or disprove the theorem.

Limitations: This is an author-reported analysis in an arXiv v1 preprint; peer review and independent specialist consensus were not established.; The paper compares selected proof components and cited Lean declarations; it does not establish that the underlying Navier–Stokes blow-up theorem is false.; For Lemma 8.6, the authors identify a specific m+4 versus m+5 derivative requirement in the manuscript and cited Lean estimate. For pressure-flux equation (10.19), they report a different bound involving localized gradient norm A_R. They also note one similar auxiliary estimate is not directly used in the proposed theorem; impact on the complete theorem dependency path remains unresolved.; No independent reproduction of the reported estimate comparison or audit of later upstream revisions was performed.

Open evidence gaps: No independent reproduction of the reported m+4/m+5 or pressure-flux estimate comparisons, and no reconciliation against later OpenAI repository revisions, were completed as of this review.; The preprint does not refute the underlying blow-up theorem. It reports selected formal correspondence gaps; the effect on the theorem’s actual proof dependencies remains unresolved, especially because the authors note one similar auxiliary bound is not directly used in the theorem.
Sources: https://arxiv.org/html/2610.08144v1
agents_memory

items: EDGEGEN reports gains from specification-derived edge-case tasks for tool-calling agents — importance 5/10 · EDGEGEN extracts compliance rules from an agent specification, combines structured rule-violation scenarios with executable database states, and uses the generated tasks for fine-tuning or harness optimization. The authors report improvement over the base model in all 18 model–benchmark comparisons across three benchmarks; on tau2-bench Airline they report relative mean-progress gains ranging from 2% to 42%, while one harness-optimization result for Gemma-4-e4b is 10% above human-curated and 30% above the base harness. Main evaluations use only 10–15 scenarios per benchmark. In a small audit, human reviewers confirmed only 6 of 10 Airline and 4 of 10 ToolSandbox runs labeled successful. These are preprint-reported results, not independently reproduced evidence of general agent reliability. — FCMO-89DF6E8A7BC3

EvoOntology reports gains from queryable semantic state and a regression-blocking evolution gate — importance 5/10 · EvoOntology presents an MCP-served ontology that data agents can query at runtime and refine through typed edits admitted only after paired evaluation on held-out tasks. On three data-agent benchmarks, the authors report improvements over no-ontology baselines across multiple backbones. On DDR-Bench, the paper reports a mean Trajectory-Wise gain of 12.3 percentage points from the initial ontology and another 7.7 points after self-evolution; on BIRD, initial ontology improves execution accuracy by 5.1 points and evolution adds 3.7. In an ablation averaged across four backbones, removing the paired gate lowers the final DDR-Bench score from 89.5 to 78.3 (-11.2 points), the largest drop among four loop components. These are author-reported results from a single preprint; no independent reproduction is reported here. — FCMO-17E52DF2A714

State-conditioned evidence sets improve coding-agent retrieval in author-reported tests — importance 4/10 · A September 2026 preprint defines retrieval for coding agents as recovering the evidence still missing from a captured decision state, and introduces SERBench. On 500 held-out states from 45 repositories, the authors report 73.0% complete evidence-set recovery at five source items versus 61.4% for Qwen3 embedding with reranking. A matched three-call similarity-only control reaches 66.6%, isolating a reported contribution from set-level selection. The benchmark, scorer and method code are released, while certificates remain in a separate organizer evaluator. Results are paper-reported and have not been independently reproduced here. — FCMO-4ADCD4C379FD

NostrAgent combines decentralized agent identity, scoped delegation, trust attestations and Lightning payment — importance 4/10 · The paper proposes NostrAgent, which places agent identity declarations, narrowing delegation chains and peer attestations in signed Nostr events, with Lightning HTTP 402 payment bound to agent identity. Its Python prototype reports depth-4 delegation verification at 0.0619 ms median (900 measurements) and a full L402 flow at 157.4 ms median (90 runs) on a local Docker regtest setup. The authors say 17 of 19 failure modes passed empirical tests, one was bounded analytically and one remains an architectural limitation. These are author-reported prototype results: experiments used a fixed seed on Apple Silicon/macOS with Python 3.11, and the linked replication package was not run independently. The paper also reports trust-query latency rising to 2.42 seconds at 500 synthetic nodes and identifies public attestation metadata and relay-consistency limits. — FCMO-0F8FFE5721F7

blocks.text: architectures_scaling

items: Cache-to-Cache reports faster cross-model communication through direct KV-cache transfer — importance 5/10 · The Cache-to-Cache (C2C) paper proposes transferring a source model’s key/value cache into a target model through a learned fuser, bypassing text generation between models. Across four question-answering benchmarks and several Qwen, Llama and Gemma combinations, the authors report 6.4–14.2% higher average accuracy than individual models and about 3.1–5.4% above text-to-text handoffs; latency was 2.5× faster on average in their tested settings. Their detailed timing table reports 3.46×, 1.51× and 14.41× speedups over text handoff for three model pairs. The fuser uses trainable pair-specific components, and scaling to many communicating models with O(N) training cost remains open. These are paper-reported results; no independent reproduction was performed. — FCMO-A1E08E02B043

blocks.text: compute_hardware

items: Apple introduces a 512 GB M5 Ultra desktop and claims faster RDMA-cluster inference — importance 5/10 · Apple’s Sept. 22, 2026 newsroom update makes Mac Studio systems with M5 Ultra available and lists configurations with up to 512 GB unified memory and 1.2 TB/s memory bandwidth. Apple also says Thunderbolt 5 with RDMA enables multiple Mac Studio systems to deliver up to 3× the distributed-inference performance of one system. The product specifications and release are first-party facts; the speedup is an Apple claim whose exact model, cluster size, metric and power/cost basis are not specified in the inspected page. No independent benchmark or matched cost analysis was performed. — FCMO-686934293815

items: A mathematical-analysis preprint reports mismatches between OpenAI’s Navier-Stokes proof and cited Lean estimates — importance 6/10 · Bastounis, Circelli and Hansen compare OpenAI’s natural-language Navier–Stokes proof with cited Lean declarations. For Lemma 8.6, equation (8.19), they report that the manuscript states an m+4 derivative estimate while the cited Lean estimate requires m+5. For pressure-flux equation (10.19), they report a different Lean bound and proof route, including an additional localized gradient norm. They note one similar auxiliary bound in the repository does not appear to be directly used in the proposed theorem, leaving the effect on the actual proof dependency chain unresolved. The authors explicitly do not claim the natural-language blow-up proof is incorrect. This remains a source-reported critique in an arXiv preprint, without independent reproduction or established specialist consensus. — FCMO-2DD7299410CB

A nested component-attribution method reports sparse, transferable circuits and a refusal edit — importance 5/10 · A September 2026 preprint proposes Matryoshka Attribution (MAttr), a learned ordering of model components based on nested masks optimized for downstream loss. The authors say it ranks first on the official Mechanistic Interpretability Benchmark leaderboard and identifies sparse, task-transferable circuits. As one application, they report that restoring 1% of Llama 3.1 8B Instruct weights to the base-model state removes refusals while maintaining capabilities. These are author claims from the preprint abstract; this activation did not inspect the full evaluation, verify the leaderboard or reproduce the intervention. — FCMO-6424926E404B

An energy-aware model router reports a measured accuracy–energy tradeoff across seven benchmarks — importance 5/10 · A September 2026 arXiv paper evaluates a learned router that selects among nine open-weight models using accuracy, latency, power and GPU-energy signals. On a held-out replay set of 913 questions across seven benchmarks, the authors report UniRoute accuracy of 0.618 at 2,192.2 J per answer and a KL-GRPO checkpoint at accuracy 0.609 and 1,691.9 J, about 23% lower answer energy. They describe a phase transition near 60% accuracy. The measurements use A100-SXM4-80GB GPUs and GPU energy; the headline comparison does not include router energy, which is discussed separately. This is a paper-reported result for a local-serving regime, not independent reproduction or production deployment evidence. — FCMO-C63BEF968F0B

A robotics paper shows hidden cross-module error dependence can break downstream uncertainty calibration — importance 5/10 · A September 20, 2026 arXiv paper analyzes how uncertainty estimates from separately calibrated robotic modules can fail when combined if their errors are correlated. It studies a two-module moving-obstacle example in which position and velocity errors share fixed Gaussian marginals while their correlation varies. The authors report that individual 95% coverage stayed near nominal, but downstream coverage under an independence assumption ranged from 99.98% at correlation -0.9 to 86.46% at +0.9. In a simulated crossing controller, positive dependence increased collisions to 39.7 per 10,000 trials under the independence interface versus 8.7 with oracle joint covariance; joint-covariance estimation restored coverage near 95%, while robust bounds reduced risk at a conservatism cost. This is a controlled simulation result, not evidence of failure rates in physical robots or deployed stacks. — FCMO-6856948EC174

Trajectory-aware selection reports lower-error SWE-agent regression estimates at one-tenth benchmark size — importance 5/10 · A September 21, 2026 paper proposes selecting a small regression-test subset for software-engineering agents from prior task outcomes and sanitized trajectory embeddings. Across 76 configurations and three code-agent regression scenarios using SWE-Bench Verified and SWE-Rebench, the authors report that their 10% deterministic subset kept median resolve-rate estimation error below 5% and reduced token consumption from 3.44 billion to about 345 million in the analyzed multi-model runs. They analyze 31,779 trajectories from 58 runs across five agent frameworks and use temporal splits so selection uses earlier runs than evaluation runs. The method requires prior full-run history, dataset-specific trajectory sanitization and refresh when behavior changes; evidence is limited to code-repair benchmarks and the paper has no independent reproduction in this record. — FCMO-5ADDBE3E1281

BackTrend reports that current research agents recover few validated scientific weak signals in a retrospective benchmark — importance 5/10 · BackTrend is a retrospective benchmark built from 25 mature AI/ML topics and 66 human-validated early problem- and solution-space signals, with systems restricted to evidence available by the end of 2023. Across seven evaluated LLM, RAG and agentic systems, the authors report maximum semantic-judge F1 of 10.1% and Coverage@10 of 18.5%; deeper retrieval helps some systems, while unlimited search can reduce performance. In a sample of 100 unmatched predictions, two annotators judged 49% and 57% plausible, suggesting the reference set may omit valid signals and benchmark F1 can understate performance. The authors report a useful retrospective evaluation result, not evidence that current systems have or lack prospective scientific foresight. — FCMO-F323BAA47595

DUMA-Bench reports higher agent attack success in dual-control tests, with a paper–artifact mismatch — importance 5/10 · DUMA-Bench introduces executable security scenarios in which an agent and user simulator can both shape a changing environment. The paper reports higher attack success under dual-control than solo evaluation (41.1% vs 26.9%), but the linked repository README currently displays 40.3% vs 25.4% over 1,960 trials per regime. That paper–artifact difference has not been reconciled. The comparison also changes multi-turn interaction, user activity and environment evolution together, so it is a regime-level robustness gap rather than an isolated causal estimate of user influence. State assertions are deterministic, while communication assertions use GPT-4o judging. — FCMO-F38D91B91495

Anthropic and Accenture announce a directly funded embedded evaluation partnership — importance 5/10 · On Sept. 18, 2026, Anthropic announced a non-exclusive partnership with Accenture’s Faculty business to evaluate and red-team models, assess alignment, and test safeguards. Each organization said it expects to invest at least $1 billion over five years to build capacity. Evaluators are intended to work inside AI companies with access comparable to employees, including observation of training and deployment decisions and direct staff interviews. Anthropic said access and reporting standards, and a settled funding model for independent evaluation, do not yet exist; it will directly fund this partnership while exploring pilots with nonprofit evaluators. This is evidence of an announced organizational model and planned investment, not evidence that evaluations are operating or independent in practice. — FCMO-0F178F944930

blocks.text: inference_systems

items: Disaggregated quantization specializes prefill and decode for reported LLM efficiency gains — importance 5/10 · A September 2026 preprint proposes separate quantization choices for prompt prefill and token-by-token decoding, arguing that the two phases have different compute and memory bottlenecks. On released Qwen3.8-27B GGUF decoders, the authors report that an NVFP4 prefiller improved 1-bit results by 32.5 points on MMLU-Pro and 35.3 on MMMU-Pro without changing the decode checkpoint. In an 8K-prompt test on the same 27B model, SSD-offloaded disaggregated prefill reportedly reduced time to first token by 1.78× versus weight-only inference. These are author-reported results under particular model, quantization and serving conditions; no independent reproduction was performed here. — FCMO-FAF16B248584

BarrierFormer reports predictive safety control with low simulated inference latency — importance 5/10 · BarrierFormer trains a causal transformer to predict short state rollouts and enforce control-barrier constraints through a training-time safety teacher, removing online optimization at inference. The authors compare it with four reimplemented baselines across a double integrator, Dubins car and Crazyflie simulator, using 32 environments and three seeds. Their learned-dynamics variant reports 95.83%–96.88% safety on two 2D systems and 96.88% on the 3D system, with per-step batched inference around 4.79–5.12 microseconds on one workstation. This is a simulation result: training still uses a black-box simulator, performance degrades as complexity rises, and the authors warn of a potentially large simulation-to-real gap. — FCMO-2B00C06542B1

FoldQuantVLA reports faster low-bit inference for vision-language-action policies with small-task robot results — importance 5/10 · The authors introduce FoldQuantVLA, which keeps activation coordinate transforms consistent across calibration, quantized weight rounding and TensorRT execution. On GR00T N1.5/N1.6/N1.7 and π₀.₅, they report W4A4 projection speedups of 1.20–1.33× over floating-point TensorRT on Jetson AGX Orin and 1.25–1.52× on a desktop RTX 4070 Ti SUPER. A selective W8A8 setting for two language projections adds 1 ms to the N1.7 Orin path and reports 92.5% pooled success versus 80.0% for uniform W4A4 across 80 physical-robot trials. These are author-reported measurements: selective-precision gains were not resolved in their LIBERO controls, robot trials were small, and latency measurements used one timing run. — FCMO-D7EAA36CAACC

Conduit turns distributed RL experience handling into a runtime optimization surface — importance 5/10 · Zhang et al. present Conduit, an Experience Data Plane that separates reinforcement-learning experience ingestion, placement and delivery from framework execution. The authors report up to 97% lower exposed experience-path latency and up to 38% lower end-to-end iteration latency in RLlib tests spanning DQN, SAC and PPO workloads on an eight-actor/eight-learner setup. They also report scaling from 8 to 1,024 AMD MI250X GPUs on a fixed workload, compared with Conduit without adaptive placement, and similar convergence curves in two tested tasks. These are author-reported results from one preprint, not an independent reproduction; transfer to other workloads and full cost/energy effects remain unmeasured. — FCMO-186CC6B3799E

NVIDIA pairs an agent-guided ROS 2 migration workflow with buffer-backed GPU transport — importance 5/10 · NVIDIA's Sep. 22, 2026 Isaac ROS 5.0 materials add agent-ready robotics workflows and describe using an AI-guided skill to migrate a Depth Anything 3 TensorRT node to ROS 2 Lyrical's rosidl::Buffer with a CUDA backend. ROS 2 documentation supports buffer-backed uint8[] message fields, while the upstream CUDA backend README describes same-host/same-GPU/same-user IPC and CPU fallback elsewhere. NVIDIA's tutorial presents an implementation and a verification recipe, but this review found no measured end-to-end performance result for that node migration. — FCMO-0BFE40B73887

blocks.text: labs_industry

items: Meta releases Muse Wonder and Wonder Full with a 1M-token context and broad agent evaluations — importance 5/10 · Meta released Muse Wonder and Muse Wonder Full on October 12, 2026. Its research post describes both as models for personal and professional agent tasks, while the linked model card lists a 1M-token inference context and evaluations spanning agent work, coding, and general capability. The models are available through Meta's API and Muse Code, with Wonder Full limited to Muse Code subscribers. Meta reports state-of-the-art benchmark performance, but the model card says it selects the highest available result where comparable results differ and that its internally run comparisons against proprietary competitors are best-effort. This is evidence of a substantial model release and of Meta's reported evaluation, not independent confirmation of broad capability leadership; a fuller safety report is still forthcoming. — FCMO-1AFA3EFAE2B1

items: EgoWild2Dex reports transferring in-the-wild human video to bimanual robot manipulation with limited robot data — importance 6/10 · The authors present EgoWild2Dex, which aligns egocentric human observations with robot views and trains a dexterous manipulation policy through broad human-data pretraining, task-specific human–robot co-training and robot-domain refinement. Their EgoWild corpus contains 538.9 hours, 179,049 episodes and 125,961 task descriptions. On three long-horizon bimanual tasks, the authors report 90%–100% success using less than one hour of robot demonstrations per task; object-level success on three unseen package contents is 30%–40%. GeoFormer image alignment is reported at 7.43 ms mean latency versus 162.58 ms for a projection-and-inpainting baseline, excluding image decoding and model loading. These are author-reported results from a limited task and robot setting; the paper says the data, models and code will be released and still requires robot fine-tuning. — FCMO-BF6ACF1C950B

CHOREO reports long-horizon composition of heterogeneous humanoid skills through a shared trajectory interface — importance 5/10 · A September 11, 2026 arXiv paper introduces CHOREO, which converts motion clips, pretrained RL rollouts and generated motions into a shared trajectory representation, then composes them with tracker-aware boundary matching and validated bridge motions. In a matched Unitree G1 MuJoCo benchmark of 130 fixed sequences, the authors report 124/130 successful sequences (95.4%), including 45/48 eight-action sequences (93.8%), compared with 20/48 (41.7%) for the strongest listed baseline. The paper reports one execution per task, no physical-robot tests, and closed-loop rollout for only 356 of 3,069 registered source assets. This is a potentially useful modular robotics result, not evidence of reliable real-world or open-ended humanoid autonomy. — FCMO-8B7403E55F68

GLIDE reports that executable guardrails improve manipulation demonstrations and selected robot-policy trials — importance 5/10 · GLIDE is a framework that generates executable command guardrails from task descriptions, refines them using teleoperation trajectories and reuses them during policy execution. Across three dual-arm manipulation tasks, the authors report that GLIDE guardrails raise teleoperation success to 70%, 90% and 90%, compared with 0%, 10% and 0% under unguarded teleoperation and 20%, 60% and 60% under domain-expert hardcoded guardrails. In 10-trial policy conditions, runtime guardrails improve two success-only-trained tasks but reduce wine-serving success from 50% to 40%; mixed-quality GLIDE data with filtering reaches 70%, 60% and 60%. The paper reports a bounded physical-robot study, not general safety or broad task transfer. The authors provide a public runtime repository and demonstration datasets, which were not independently run or analyzed here. — FCMO-9E51A9966402

Perseverance driving data supports paper-reported multimodal traversability learning on an Earth-analog rover — importance 4/10 · A September 21 arXiv paper introduces a multimodal traversability estimator trained from about 500 sols and 45 km of Mars 2020 Perseverance driving data. On 35 held-out sols, the authors report AUROC 0.874, average precision 0.878 and F1 0.758, above the strongest listed baseline (0.816, 0.802 and 0.602); means are reported across five seeds. They also describe integrating the learned hazard map into modified ENav flight software and testing it on an Earth-analog rover, primarily on flat ground with large rocks. These are paper-reported results. The linked project page says code and dataset are forthcoming; no independent reproduction or Mars deployment is established. — FCMO-079A8366CDDF

blocks.text: reasoning_posttraining

items: Policy-aligned critic training reports gains on mathematical reasoning and software tasks — importance 5/10 · A September 2026 preprint formalizes token-level credit using three stated regularity conditions and proposes Policy Aligned Critic Training (PACT), which trains the critic after the actor and applies importance-sampling correction. The authors report 72.87% average accuracy across four agentic mathematical-reasoning benchmarks, 8.80 and 13.16 percentage points above GRPO and PPO, respectively; on SWE-bench Verified they report 67.4%, 2.4 points above PPO. These are paper-reported results under the authors’ training and evaluation setup, not independent confirmation of a general post-training improvement. — FCMO-AC0F53478D3D

Paired rollout schedules reduce reward noise, but do not guarantee better agent learning — importance 5/10 · The Sep. 21 arXiv paper analyzes paired, event-keyed environment schedules for group-relative reinforcement learning of tool-using agents. Its theory shows that pairing removes the shared environment-noise component from sibling reward contrasts but can still increase gradient variance under some score geometries. In a registered study using one Qwen3.5-2B agent and three seeds per design, pairing improved noisy-test success under transient tool faults by 5.1 points but missed the registered learning-curve criterion; under grader flips, the learning-curve difference was small and uncertain. A finite probe found lower gradient covariance traces, but the result is limited to eight checkpoints from two trajectories and does not establish broad learning gains. — FCMO-46CA1670BFE8

items: Anthropic reports layered defenses cut observed reasoning extraction by 10–100× — importance 5/10 · In an Oct. 12, 2026 research post, Anthropic describes layered defenses against attempts to extract Claude reasoning for unauthorized model distillation. The company reports that, after full deployment, reasoning tokens it identified as extracted by distillers on its own platform were consistently 10 to 100 times lower than before; it also says its two-stage classifier caught the extraction techniques described in its September report. This is a provider-reported operational measure, not an independent efficacy evaluation. Anthropic says it has not yet seen a highly sophisticated persistent attempt against the defenses, expects attackers to adapt, and reports integration changes, a benign-request false-positive rate below 0.1%, and charging for some blocked requests. — FCMO-479F1F4F0228
